There are a few basic categories of scientific article out there, and none of them lend themselves to crowdsourcing of author credit. What @CANCEL-CAT-FACTS linked is crowdsourced participation, but not authorship. Here are the general types of paper you could consider writing:

1) Experimental.

Here you're looking to create a controlled environment where you can complete some experimental manipulation. Where are you going to be running these subjects? Someone's got to have a lab, which significantly undercuts the decentralized plan you're going for. That is, unless you plan on using the online services like Mechanical Turk. And even if you use MT, there's the issue of creating the test and analyzing the data. Who among your group understands which measures are scientifically meaningful, and knows the necessary statistical tools to make those measures?

Not to mention, how do you agree on a consistent experimental design that appropriately addresses your research question? Some of the interested participants may be experts, but how to you make sure that their helpful contribution doesn't get lost in the sea of voices? And if a small group actually knows what to do, why aren't they just doing a normal collaborative study like all the others we see published?

2) Meta-analytic

So rather than do an experiment, you could analyze the results of others. This is easy, in the sense that it's just math. But "just math" is a level of math taught only in advanced mathematics departments at universities, or taught to the very Masters and PhD students you're trying to cut out of the process. So who among your group knows the math, and knows the material well enough to conduct the analysis. Once again, you run into the "small number does all the work" problem.

3) Literature review

Easily the most accessible to those who have less formal training in a field. But at the same time, does not lend itself to a group effort. In order to complete a comprehensive literature review, you'd need to be extremely well versed in the existing research. Most of the time, the best teacher is experience. But if not, why would you expect dozens of contributors to all reach the same incredibly-high level of understanding when one or two could do the job just as easily and without the complication of lots of co-authors?
